data.title: Fierce Pharma Week: Top trends, campaigns and conversations
data.description:
Fierce Pharma Week brought thousands of people to Philadelphia for four days of conversations about pharma marketing, commercialization, medical affairs and communications.

In this episode of "The Top Line," Fierce editors share the conversations, trends and moments that stood out from the event. Topics include Genentech’s use of humor and celebrity storytelling to raise awareness of diabetic macular edema, how Novo is navigating the extraordinary attention around GLP-1 drugs, and the growing role of AI in pharma marketing. The team also looks at some of the campaigns honored at the Fierce Pharma Marketing Awards and the creative approaches companies are using to reach patients and healthcare professionals.

To learn more about the topics in this episode: 

  • ‘People like the sincerity of it’: comedian Damon Wayans on humor, relatability and DME awareness in…
  • Standout pharma marketing takes the stage at the 2026 Fierce Pharma Marketing Awards
  • Panthers and zebras and meerkats, oh my: A peek behind the curtain at Fierce Pharma Week 2026
  • Former 'Real Housewives' star Jenn Fessler and CineHealth’s Tracey Yaw break down authentic healthca…
  • 'The growth driver of our organization'; Genentech CMO Zoë Lazarre on experimental marketing, AI and…
  • Journalist and menopause advocate Tamsen Fadal shines a light on overlooked women’s health topics

data.title: Eli Lilly blasted for ‘emotive’ language in GLP-1 press release
data.description:
A U.K. watchdog has scolded Eli Lilly over a press release the drugmaker sent to the BBC, arguing that its use of “promotional and emotive” language brought discredit on the pharma industry. 

The PMCPA, the U.K. self-regulatory body for pharma marketing, took up the case after a complainant shared a BBC article about Lilly’s oral GLP-1 receptor agonist orforglipron. The article reported phase 3 data on orforglipron. While the drug is now sold as Foundayo, the small molecule was yet to come to market at the time of the article, leading the complainant to accuse Lilly of pre-license promotion. 

Because the BBC article was written by an independent journalist, the PMCPA focused its investigation on the Lilly press release that informed the story. The press release, which Lilly sent to the health editor at BBC News, included phrases such as “transform obesity care” that the PMCPA ruled “went beyond the provision of factual, non-promotional information relating to clinical trial data.”

The PMCPA panel concluded that the “cumulative effect of the language used in the press release, in the context of its audience,” meant that the Lilly document promoted orforglipron before the grant of its marketing authorization. Pre-license promotion is prohibited under the code enforced by the PMCPA. 

That finding led the PMCPA to rule that Lilly had breached two other clauses of the code. By neglecting to notice that “the positive language used in the quotations was promotional, in the context of its foreseeable audience,” Lilly failed to maintain high standards, the PMCPA said. Based on those issues, the PMCPA ruled Lilly had brought discredit upon, and reduced confidence in, the industry. 

Lilly appealed. The drugmaker argued that the PMCPA panel “placed undue emphasis on selectively extracted wording [and] failed to consider the communication in its full context.” Lilly noted that while the PMCPA focused on the words “transform obesity care,” the full phrase said it is “working to transform obesity care.” The full phrase “is clearly forward-looking and aspirational in nature,” Lilly said.

More broadly, Lilly argued that the rulings were inconsistent with “established PMCPA practice and fundamental legal principles of certainty and proportionality.” The drugmaker warned the PMCPA about rulings that, in its view, extended the scope of the code in an unpredictable and unclear manner. 

“The suggestion that routine engagement with journalists, or the use of measured and evidence-based language in communicating clinical data, may give rise to findings of promotion or discredit introduces an unwarranted degree of uncertainty for companies committed to complying with the code,” Lilly said.

Lilly lost the appeal. The appeal board largely reiterated the original panel’s conclusions. The proactive dissemination of a press release with promotional and emotive language to a mainstream media outlet with a broad public reach promoted orforglipron before licensing, the board said. Having adopted that view, the board found Lilly had failed to maintain high standards and brought discredit upon the industry. 

Lilly didn’t respond immediately to a request for comment on the PMCPA case.

data.title: Former reality star Jenn Fessler on healthcare storytelling
data.description:
“Bravolebrity” Jenn Fessler knows a thing or two about authenticity. It’s how she made a name for herself as a podcaster and TV personality, with her candid honesty and humorous commentary standing out during her stint on Bravo’s “The Real Housewives of New Jersey.”

That same authenticity, Fessler says, is key to breaking through to audiences in healthcare communications. Sharing stories about real-life experiences on digital platforms that transcend traditional advertising and education channels can build trust and drive awareness and education to new levels as the influence of social media spaces continues to grow.  

Fessler joined CineHealth festival director Tracey Yaw, National CineMedia’s Manu Singh, screenwriter and Avalere Health’s chief creative officer, U.S. marketing TJ Cimfel and Jeff Fischer of Publicis Health Media in a panel at Fierce Pharma Week to dive into the empowering impact of audio, film and digital content. 

“There’s something about the humanity of it all,” Fessler told Fierce Pharma Marketing in an interview, referring to sharing health stories across virtual platforms. “It’s sharing experiences and sharing strength.” 

With the plethora of platforms primed for health-related discussions, from social media to radio to podcasting and more, “we’re getting closer to true communication,” Fessler said. “Like real humanity, connecting with someone’s humanity and their story, and for me, that’s just the most impactful way to learn.”

Related

Standout pharma marketing takes the stage at the 2026 Fierce Pharma Marketing Awards

Engaging with these stories can make a difference on the patient side, as education and research into other people’s experiences is an important component to self-advocacy. As a patient, one often must “be your own healthcare CEO,” Yaw added in the interview, quoting Emmy-winning journalist Maria Menudos. Menudos was awarded CineHealth’s 2026 Lifetime Achievement Award at the Fierce Pharma Marketing Awards gala in recognition of her bravery in sharing her stories of battling two different types of cancer. 

“When you talk to other people and you hear that stories, that changes everything,” Yaw said. 

Platforms traditionally used as “entertainment venues” such as in TV, radio, and podcasting are not only where stories are being told but where they’re “really, really listened to,” Fessler explained. Social media in particular has a unique advantage of reaching multiple generations, as even information targeted to a younger audience can reach their older relatives through them. 

However, considering that over 50% of Gen Z’s get their healthcare information from TikTok, “we have to be really careful about what’s out there,” Yaw warned, especially with occasionally inaccurate AI and misinformation on the rise. Still, stories shared on social media can be a starting point for consumers to gather more information before making healthcare decisions, she noted. 

To make health stories feel authentic and lived-in, Fessler explains that it’s all in “the dirty details.” 

Throughout her time on reality television, Fessler was “very quick” to be open about medication and mental health, she said. More recently, she’s told medical tales she deems “not pretty,” such as her experience with GI side effects of GLP-1s. 

Those types of stories are “stigmatized,” she explained, which makes them particularly important to share. 

“It’s impactful when you stop judging your stories, and you're willing to dig a little deeper, and you're willing to open up a little bit more about the stuff that is stigmatized,” Fessler said. “I always think that's powerful.” 

Authenticity, Yaw notes, is backed by an “emotion and passion” that may not exist without lived experience. When celebrity spokespeople or actors are hired to speak about a condition or treatment that they don’t have real experience with, “you can tell a difference,” she said, making trust harder to come by. 

As a content creator herself, Fessler values “feeling the impact” of her stories and stays away from partnerships she doesn’t personally believe in. 

Related

How pharma marketers are capturing the power of podcasts to connect with consumers

For four years now, CineHealth has shone a spotlight on innovative storytelling in the health and wellness space as the only international film festival that focuses exclusivity on these topics. Yaw is “so passionate about this and being able to bring people's stories to life and giving them a platform,” she said. This year, the winner’s slate included standout contributions across feature films, short films, episodic series, social media shorts and podcasts. 

Outside of her work at CineHealth, Yaw works at healthcare consulting firm Avelere Health as its director of operations, media. Avelere makes content that goes “beyond just a commercial,” Yaw said. 

Avalere’s work with argenx on “CIDP Unscripted” swept the stage at the Fierce Pharma Marketing Awards gala, earning a CineHealth award in the episodic series category plus a Fierce Pharma Marketing win in both the Online Video or Film and Website for Consumer slots. “CIDP Unscripted” is an online learning video series that highlights the unpredictability of chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) by partnering with renowned improv troupe the Upright Citizens Brigade. The fun yet educational videos present practical improv tools that patients can harness to build confidence and better communicate with their doctors and families.

data.title: GSK slammed for grossly misleading, totally unacceptable actions
data.description:
GSK showed a “totally unacceptable” lack of transparency in its interactions with the PMCPA, the U.K. self-regulatory body ruled.

The PMCPA originally investigated whether a GSK video about a shingles vaccination program broke U.K. rules on advertising prescription-only medicines to the public. GSK successfully defended itself against all the allegations. After reaching its conclusions, but before releasing its findings, the PMCPA sent the case report to the U.K. Health Security Agency (UKHSA) as a courtesy because it was named in the document.

That is when the heat on GSK intensified. The UKHSA responded to the PMCPA to suggest that extracts of minutes that GSK cited in its defense failed to accurately reflect its engagement with the drugmaker. After receiving materials from the UKHSA, the PMCPA opened a new case centered on GSK’s disclosures. The second case went against GSK.

“The panel was seriously concerned about GSK’s conduct in [the original case], including its conduct at the appeal board hearing and its failure to provide a full and frank disclosure,” the PMCPA said. “GSK’s lack of transparency, which had only come to light due to [the] UKHSA contacting the PMCPA, was totally unacceptable.”

In an emailed statement, a GSK spokesperson said the company is “committed to upholding the highest standards of integrity and ethical conduct in all aspects of our business, including adherence to industry codes and regulations.” The spokesperson added that GSK supports the principles and requirements of self-regulation, including transparency and the PMCPA’s role, and ran the shingles campaign in good faith.

“With regards to the report’s findings, while there was no intention to mislead the PMCPA, we recognize that greater information and context could have been provided and we regret and apologize for this,” the spokesperson said.

The PMCPA ruled that GSK failed to maintain high standards when providing materials to inform the original case. The rulings centered on whether GSK accurately represented the information it received about the UKHSA’s approval—or lack thereof—of the shingles vaccination awareness campaign.

GSK gave the PMCPA minutes of its meeting with the UKHSA, only cutting, in its words, “unrelated topics and personal identifiers.” When the PMCPA received the full minutes, it saw that GSK had cut a section in which the UKHSA “emphasized the importance of maintaining a professional distance, reflective of the independent nature of each organization.” The PMCPA ruled that GSK erred by cutting the information. 

Another PMCPA finding related to an email exchange between GSK and the UKHSA. Four weeks before the PMCPA ruled on the original case, the UKHSA emailed GSK to say that “it is not within our remit to give any formal approvals and we have not provided this function.” The agency added that it was clear from the outset that it “would not be able to endorse” any materials. 

GSK never told the PMCPA about the exchange. After finding out about the email, the PMCPA ruled that the company’s nondisclosure represented a failure to maintain high standards. The PMCPA called GSK’s failure to share the email with the appeal board for the original case “grossly misleading.”

Other findings covered GSK’s exchanges with the appeal board handling the original case. GSK told the PMCPA that it “consistently and accurately stated that it had never asserted that [the] UKHSA was providing formal ministerial approval.” The PMCPA panel called GSK’s claim “wholly disingenuous,” citing the drugmaker’s written and verbal statements to support its conclusions. 

While GSK expressed regrets to PMCPA about certain aspects of its handling of the original case, it sought to overturn most of the findings on appeal. GSK argued that it selected extracts from the meeting minutes in good faith, and that it did not consider the UKHSA email to represent “a settled or authoritative position.”

GSK found no evidence that the decision not to disclose the UKHSA email was a deliberate attempt to mislead, telling the PMCPA that it needed to investigate the conflict between its understanding and the health agency’s position. The PMCPA appeal board called GSK’s decision “totally unreasonable” and took GSK to task for the actions. 

“The appeal board was particularly concerned by the positive decisions made by GSK’s representatives to not provide or refer to crucial correspondence that GSK had had with UKHSA that was unambiguously contradictory to the company’s submissions. To claim confusion for this decision was disingenuous,” the PMCPA said. “The appeal board questioned the culture within GSK in this regard.”

GSK was publicly reprimanded by the PMCPA.

data.title: How Learning Systems Move Pharma Marketing Beyond the Box Score
data.description:
AI is already changing how pharma marketers work, from summarizing research to analyzing campaign performance and identify patterns, so brands can make decisions faster. Those wins matter, but they’re only the start of what’s possible.

Think about baseball. Teams once relied heavily on box scores and scouting reports to shape future player and game decisions. Today, AI can analyze far more data, uncover patterns, and build a much smarter starting lineup. But what happens when the starting pitcher gets pulled in the third inning, or the expected power hitter can’t catch up to a fastball?

The best teams do not simply follow a smarter pregame plan. They adjust as the game unfolds, and pharma marketing needs to do the same.

From Looking Back to Looking Ahead

For decades, marketing analytics have been largely retrospective. We identify who prescribed. Measure who engaged. Determine which channels performed. Analyze what drove conversion. Then use those findings to make the next campaign a little better than the last.

AI helps us tackle a different set of questions. Which patients may be approaching a meaningful milestone in their care journey? Which providers are likely to encounter those patients? Which HCPs may be most receptive to new information? When might engagement be particularly relevant?

Imagine seeing signals suggesting that an HCP is likely to see several brand-eligible patients in the coming weeks. That changes not just who to reach, but when—and the prescribing response becomes new information for the next decision.

Healthcare is inherently dynamic. Patients move through diagnoses, treatment decisions, therapy changes, and access challenges, while an HCP’s relevance changes with the patients entering their care. And a static plan, even a very smart one, cannot fully reflect that reality.

Predict. Activate. Learn. Repeat. 

Marketers’ greatest AI opportunity is connecting individual predictions to build better decision systems. An HCP who engages with educational content may become more relevant for future outreach. An HCP repeatedly reached during relevant care windows who does not change behavior may become less of a priority. A prescribing outcome can help refine future audience selection. Even an expected behavior that never materializes can teach the system something.

The output of one decision becomes the input to the next, creating compounding intelligence that improves future decisions.

Solving the Right Problems

There’s an important caveat, however: adding AI does not automatically create intelligent marketing.

A model can be highly accurate and still solve the wrong problem. For example, predicting who is likely to click an ad is very different from predicting which HCP may soon encounter a clinically appropriate treatment opportunity. In pharma, the usefulness of AI depends as much on the question being asked as the sophistication of the model answering it. If good intelligence compounds, bad assumptions can compound too.

That means marketers need to look beyond whether a platform or partner “uses AI” and ask harder questions.

  • What is the AI actually predicting? Is it recognizing changes that indicate an emerging treatment opportunity—or simply finding people who resemble past converters?
  • What data informs the prediction? Is it grounded in healthcare-specific, real-world signals or proxies for likely behavior?
  • Can the prediction change an action? Intelligence trapped in analytics and disconnected from audience planning, activation, point of care, or other channels has limited value.
  • Does the system learn from real outcomes? Without that feedback loop, AI may make a campaign smarter. With it, AI can make the marketing system smarter.

The Next AI Competitive Advantage

If the first era of data-driven marketing was about using information to make better decisions, AI opens the door to something more ambitious: connecting those decisions into systems that continually learn.

The goal is not to hand marketing strategy over to an algorithm. In a regulated, clinically complex industry, human judgment remains critical to defining objectives, choosing meaningful signals, validating predictions, establishing privacy and governance controls, and deciding where technology should (and should not) act.

But the marketers who get this right may eventually stop thinking about AI as another tool in the technology stack. Instead, they will think about intelligence as the connective tissue between data, audiences, activation, measurement, and the next decision.

Because the next AI frontier isn’t simply creating more at-bats, or even more runs. It’s learning from every plate appearance—and using that intelligence to make the next opportunity smarter.

data.title: In landmark for Korean biotech, Elevar wins FDA nod for Lyrfigtu
data.description:
The FDA came to Elevar Therapeutics bearing gift ahead of the mid-autumn festival.

The U.S. agency has approved the company’s Lyrfigtu (lirafugratinib) for patients with previously treated bile duct cancer harboring an FGFR2 gene fusion or other rearrangement. 

As Jin Yang-gon, chairman of HLB Group, Elevar’s parent company, noted in a YouTube announcement, Lyrfigtu marks the first novel cancer drug from a Korean company to secure FDA approval. 

“The greatest gift brought by this new drug approval is the newfound confidence spreading throughout the company, bolstered by the achievement of becoming a firm with a global anti-cancer drug,” Jin said during the auto English-dubbed announcement. “Our goal was to complete new drug development independently, rather than relying on technology exports, which require waiting for others to develop and produce results.”

Compared with existing FGFR inhibitors such as Incyte’s Pemazyre and Taiho’s Lytgobi, Lyrfigtu was designed with increased selectivity for FGFR2, while sparing other proteins of the FGFR family, to minimize toxicities. Elevar obtained the asset from Relay Therapeutics in 2024 for $75 million in upfront and regulatory milestone payments and up to $425 million in potential commercial milestones. 

In a single-arm trial called Refocus, Lyrfigtu registered an objective response rate of 46% and median duration of response reaching 11.8 months among 116 patients with cholangiocarcinoma new to FGFR inhibitor treatment but who had received prior chemotherapy or chemoimmunotherapy. The median progression-free survival was 11.3 months. 

“Lyrfigtu’s unique, irreversible, covalent-binding mechanism enables potent and sustained inhibition of FGFR2, including many resistance mutations that can emerge with earlier FGFR inhibitors,” Lipika Goyal, M.D., from the Stanford Cancer Center and lead author of the Refocus trial, said in a Sept. 23 announcement. “This FDA approval brings an important next-generation precision medicine option directly to patients with advanced bile duct cancer.”

Elevar expects to make Lyrfigtu to patients in the U.S. this year. The company also filed an application with the European Medicines Agency on Sept. 15, Jin said. 

Jin touted Lyrfigtu’s potential in other cancer types, including ongoing clinical trials in a tumor-agnostic setting, as well as opportunities to be combined with other anticancer drugs by Big Pharma. Now that the drug has been approved, the company expects patient enrollment in clinical trials to accelerate, Jin said.

Related

FDA rejects Hengrui, Elevar’s PD-1 liver cancer combo for a 3rd time

The milestone of an FDA approval came years late for Elevar and its parent HLB. The company’s first U.S. approval was supposed to be the combination of camrelizumab and rivoceranib, partnered with China’s Hengrui Pharma, for the first-line treatment of liver cancer. However, beginning with a pair of complete response letters in May 2024, the two drugs have been rejected three times, all because of manufacturing shortfalls at Hengrui’s facilities.

Following the most recent snub in July, Hengrui has solved the issues, and the partners are now gathering updated safety data for a resubmission, according to Jin.

data.title: Glaukos taps Stephen Curry for keratoconus awareness campaign
data.description:
Glaukos is teaming up with four-time NBA champion, two-time NBA Most Valuable Player and Olympic gold medalist Stephen Curry for a new “Could it be KC?” campaign.

Keratoconus (KC) is a progressive eye disorder in which the cornea thins and bulges outward into a cone shape.

It’s a rare disorder, with the prevalence of KC in the U.S. around 0.04%, predominantly affecting younger adults. Noticeably higher rates have been reported among Black and Hispanic populations compared with other groups.

The condition comes with a distinct lack of awareness, and thus diagnosis, as well as a high level of stigma because it can alter someone’s facial appearance.

Glaukos knows the condition well, as it markets Epioxa, an FDA-approved, noninvasive, epithelium-on corneal cross-linking treatment for KC.

Its new campaign taps Curry’s personal story of living with keratoconus. It will also more broadly serve as a disease awareness and educational campaign, with “expanding activities planned in 2027,” according to a release.

The idea is to boost recognition and earlier detection of KC while also encouraging greater uptake of treatments and procedures for the condition, all while seeking to reduce stigma.

“For a long time, I got used to just getting by, squinting and brushing off headaches, without realizing anything was wrong with my eyes,” said Curry in a statement.

“When I was diagnosed with keratoconus, it was scary, but I knew I couldn’t ignore it and asked for help. Vision is one of the biggest privileges we have, and I don’t want anyone to lose sight of what matters. My hope is that this campaign helps other individuals and families feel seen and encourages them to prioritize their eye health.”

Curry kicked off the launch by joining local students in Oakland, California, for an educational community event centered on eye health.

The event included a new picture book from Glaukos that is “inspired by Curry’s own experience living with KC,” and is set up “to make conversations about eye health and KC more approachable.” Curry read the book aloud and showed off his skills in a pickup basketball game.

There is also a new website tied to the launch that includes a quiz to see whether you or someone you know may have the condition. It also uses images and videos to show what it’s like to see with KC.

data.title: Lilly captures 70% of surging Medicare GLP-1 market, CEO says
data.description:
Sign-ups for Medicare’s GLP-1 coverage plan keep expanding, and Eli Lilly is dominating the market with 70% share, the company’s CEO David Ricks said.

Since its rollout on July 1, the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge has attracted about 700,000 seniors who’ve started treatment, Ricks said in an interview with CNBC.

The demonstration program seems to be expanding rapidly. In an Aug. 31 announcement of a new round of “most favored nation” drug pricing deals with nine biopharma companies, the White House said over 500,000 seniors had utilized the program, and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz, M.D., updated the number to 600,000 during a press conference that day.

“That’s very encouraging, that seniors are talking to their doctors. They want to manage their weight. They understand there’s long-term health consequences,” Ricks said of the program. “It’s very market expansionary, which is what we had hoped.”

The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge was launched as part of the Trump administration’s MFN deals with Lilly and Novo, offering eligible seniors GLP-1 obesity drugs at a $50 per month copay.

During the company's recent Capital Markets Day, Novo’s EVP of U.S. operations, Jamey Millar, also pointed to the Medicare program as a way to expand GLP-1 drugs’ patient base.

Related

Trump GLP-1 update teases blockbuster annual sales for Lilly from Medicare program: analyst

Lilly is capturing 7 out of 10 patients on the Medicare program, with many on its Zepbound, Ricks said. The 70% share is higher than the roughly 60% that Lilly owns in the broader obesity field, where Zepbound also takes a leading position.

“I think still we see physicians focusing on those with the most body weight and the most complications. That’s where Zepbound plays a big role,” Ricks said.

As for Lilly’s oral drug Foundayo, which lags Novo’s Wegovy pill in overall market share, Ricks said it’s attracting Medicare patients looking for convenience but not necessarily a huge weight-loss effect. Following its launch in April, Foundayo now captures about 1 out of 3 new starts for oral GLP-1 obesity drugs, and “that’s growing week over week,” according to Ricks. 

Lilly is offering its GLP-1 meds to Medicare at a net price of $245 per month. Based on a 70% market share, Jefferies analyst Akash Tewari calculated $1.4 billion in annualized revenue for the Indianapolis pharma. If the program keeps expanding at its current rate, Tewari figured Lilly could exit the year at an annualized run rate of $3 billion to $3.5 billion.

Ricks made the comments as Lilly broke ground on a new, $6.5 billion active pharmaceutical ingredient manufacturing site in Houston to produce Foundayo and other medicines. In his CNBC interview, Ricks touted the Houston facility’s ability to support Lilly’s international expansion for Foundayo.

In another potential inflection point, Foundayo is gunning for an FDA approval in Type 2 diabetes. As Ricks noted, the oral GLP-1 diabetes market is already at the same size as the obesity market.

data.title: Biogen springs kidney health campaign with gymnast Suni Lee
data.description:
Biogen has teamed with gymnast Suni Lee for a campaign, leveraging the Olympic gold medalist’s health journey and social media audience to vault deeper into kidney health awareness. 

Lee was diagnosed with two rare kidney diseases in 2023. The next year, the gymnast partnered with the American Kidney Fund on an education and awareness campaign. Lee has been “a very visible advocate for kidney health,” Lynn Leber, vice president at Biogen, told Fierce. The visibility and familiarity of Lee’s story informed Biogen’s interest in partnering with the athlete. 

“What we particularly liked about Suni was that she’s been on a very familiar journey of gathering information, managing through setbacks, then ultimately working with her healthcare team to find a treatment plan,” Leber said. 

Working through the process enabled Lee to re-enter the world of elite gymnastics. That story resonates with people living with rare kidney diseases, especially individuals with complement 3 glomerulopathy (C3G) and primary immune-complex membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (IC-MPGN), Leber said. Last year, Biogen acquired Empaveli, a treatment for C3G and IC-MPGN, in a $5.6 billion takeover.

Biogen has shared Lee’s story on its “Keep Your Momentum” website and plans to use social media to drive traffic to the page. The focus on “momentum” reflects Biogen’s intent to “encourage and inspire people that they don’t have to be held back by their disease,” Leber said. Biogen wants to “help people really see the positivity and the fact that there are options and paths forward,” the VP added. 

The campaign will feature “a series of posts coming from [Lee’s] handle, both content that she creates herself, so organic content, along with some of our own social media channels,” Leber said. Biogen will explore other channels down the line, but for now is focused on social. 

The biotech reached that decision because kidney disease patients seek information and connection on social media, and because Lee is active on the platforms, Leber said. Lee’s follower counts are 3.4 million on Instagram and 3.8 million on TikTok. The gymnast published a sponsored Biogen post on Instagram this week.

Biogen will track early indicators of the campaign’s impact using social media engagement metrics, such as clicks and views, Leber said. The biotech is also very interested in how often people are visiting its campaign website and engaging with videos and resources designed to support conversations with healthcare teams. 

Longer term, Leber plans to use focus groups and market research to assess if the campaign and related resources have led patients to have conversations with their healthcare teams and helped inform those talks.

Biogen’s work with Lee is part of a broader push into kidney disease. The campaign with Lee, which runs to mid-2027, is the “perfect partnership” for showing Biogen’s commitment to nephrology, Leber said. Nephrology could become increasingly important to Biogen as it works to grow Empaveli sales and bring kidney transplant drug candidate felzartamab to market.

data.title: AstraZeneca recommits to youth health to dial funding past $100M
data.description:
AstraZeneca has re-upped its UNICEF-partnered Young Health Programme (YHP), committing to a new five-year phase that will move total investment in the initiative above $100 million.

YHP supports young people in underserved communities. Since starting in 2010, the program has directly reached 23 million young people across more than 60 countries, AstraZeneca said. YHP has helped train more than 1 million people and “supported youth advocates to positively shape 29 laws and policies.” AstraZeneca supported the activities, including through the $35 million pledge it made in 2019.

The drugmaker aims to accelerate the program in the next five-year phase. By 2030, AstraZeneca hopes YHP will reach an additional 10 million young people, train 800,000 youth advocates and help shape 17 public policies worldwide. 

Working with more than 60 partners, AstraZeneca plans to emphasize youth-led action, health equity and climate responsiveness in the next phase of the program. The focus reflects recognition that young people are both disproportionately affected by these challenges and “powerful agents of change.”

It is unclear how much new funding AstraZeneca is providing. Total funding will exceed $100 million by 2030, but that figure includes the $35 million committed in 2019 and all other support since 2010. Even so, the available data show that the program has grown more ambitious over time. 

AstraZeneca launched (PDF) YHP in 2010 with Plan International and Johns Hopkins School of Public Health. Through the program, the company aimed to “help disconnected young people around the world understand and deal with the health issues they face.” By 2015, YHP had reached (PDF) more than 1.4 million young people, exceeding AstraZeneca’s original 1 million goal.

An expanded program underpins AstraZeneca’s belief that YHP can reach 10 times more young people in the current five-year phase than it targeted in the first five years. YHP launched in Kenya in 2016, expanded into Indonesia in 2018 and arrived in the U.K. in 2020. UNICEF joined the program in 2020.
